title: (Scenario) How would you introduce a breaking event-schema change used by 15 consumers: why must you avoid requiring fifteen teams to deploy at the same moment (use a compatibility strategy: additive evolution, a new event version, dual publication during a controlled period, or consumer changes before producer changes), and why is the technical schema only part of the problem (once fifteen teams depend on an event, changing it becomes an organizational migration)?
shortTitle: How would you introduce a breaking event-schema change used by 15 consumers?
keyPoints: Fifteen independent consumers have fifteen deployment schedules, so requiring simultaneous deployment is guaranteed to fail.
Additive evolution (add new optional fields, never remove) is the safest: old consumers ignore new fields and keep working.
For genuinely breaking changes, dual-publish v1 and v2 during a controlled deprecation window.
A schema registry with backward-compatibility enforcement rejects incompatible changes at publish time.
The technical schema is only half the problem: fifteen teams mean an organizational migration with communication, timeline, and tracking.
Always discover undocumented consumers before changing; the failure mode is 'we broke a consumer we did not know existed.'
Measure success not by how clean the new schema is, but by whether any team was forced to deploy on someone else's clock.

s1_definition.oneliner: Never force fifteen teams to deploy at one instant -- evolve additively or dual-publish a versioned event through a controlled deprecation, and treat the change as an organizational migration, not a schema edit.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Breaking Change** – a schema change where new events cannot be understood by consumers written against the old schema (removed field, changed type).
- **Additive Evolution** – only add new optional fields, never remove or rename existing ones; old consumers ignore new fields and keep working.
- **Dual Publication** – publish both v1 and v2 events during a controlled deprecation window so consumers migrate on their own schedules.
- **Schema Registry** – a central store that enforces compatibility rules, rejecting incompatible schema changes at publish time.
- **Consumer Inventory** – the set of all teams and services that consume the event, including undocumented ones.
- **Organizational Migration** – the communication, timeline, tracking, and deprecation process that gets fifteen teams across the line.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India sends a standard "transaction completed" slip to fifteen departments: fraud, statements, rewards, tax, audit, and more. Changing the slip format overnight would leave every department that has not updated its process at the same minute unable to read it. So the bank either adds new fields without removing old ones, or prints both old and new slips for a few months while each department migrates on its own schedule.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Event Schema Migration Strategy
  ───────────────────────────────

  Additive (preferred):
  Producer publishes:
    {transferId, amountMinor, currency(NEW)}    ← v1+ fields
  Old consumers:  read transferId, amountMinor  ← ignore currency
  New consumers:  read all fields               ← use currency
  No coordination needed.

  Dual Publication (breaking change):
  Producer publishes:
    Topic v1: {transferId, amountMinor}          ← old schema
    Topic v2: {transferId, amountMinor, currency} ← new schema
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Deprecation window: 3 months                │
  │ Each team migrates v1 → v2 on own schedule  │
  │ Track: 12/15 migrated, 3 remaining          │
  │ Retire v1 ONLY when 15/15 and zero readers  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A breaking event-schema change with fifteen consumers cannot be flipped in one deployment because fifteen independent teams have fifteen deployment schedules. The whole strategy is about buying time so the producer's change and each consumer's change happen on independent schedules.

The safest technique is additive evolution: add new optional fields, never remove existing ones, so old consumers keep working. For genuinely breaking changes, dual-publish v1 and v2 during a controlled deprecation window and let each team migrate on its own schedule. A schema registry with backward-compatibility enforcement rejects incompatible changes before they can break consumers.

The part that matters most is that the technical schema is only half the problem. The event is a contract with fifteen counterparties, and changing it requires discovering all consumers (including undocumented ones), publishing a deprecation timeline, tracking migration status, and retiring the old version only when confirmed at zero usage.

Remember one sentence: never force fifteen teams to deploy on one clock; evolve additively or dual-publish with a tracked deprecation, and treat the change as an organizational migration.
